Another Sticky Problem

Game StrategyParityInvariants

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)

Game: Two players take turns breaking a stick in two or removing k sticks of length k; the player who makes the last move wins.
How to play: Click a square to the right of a break line to split its stick, or press a Remove button. The computer replies at once.
Look for the math

Two sticks, of lengths N and N+1, are enough to hide a perfect strategy. The winning play only ever visits two kinds of position, and the second player can always answer in the other kind.

Breaks, removals and the last move

Start with sticks N and N+1. A move either breaks one stick into two shorter positive lengths, or removes k sticks that each have length k. The player who makes the last move wins: ordinary normal play. The game was published in 2004 as Mathematics Magazine problem #1687 (Sung Soo Kim); the two sets below are Li Zhou’s solution.

The applet offers Break and Remove as two radio modes. This page shows both at once: a click breaks, and the buttons remove. The applet’s Remove mode can take one stick fewer than k when more than k are present; this page follows the stated rule and always removes exactly k.

The two sets

Call a position A when it has an even number of sticks and at most one even-length stick. Call it B when it has an odd number of sticks and at most two even-length sticks.

The start is in A: it has two sticks, and exactly one of N and N+1 is even. The empty board is in A too: zero sticks, none of them even. A and B do not cover every possible position, but the strategy never leaves them. The two sets are really a test of parity: the number of sticks and the number of even sticks.

From A you can only reach B

Break. A break adds one stick, so the number of sticks changes from even to odd. If the broken stick was odd, its two pieces are one even and one odd (an odd number is an even plus an odd), so A’s at most one even stick becomes at most two. If it was the single even stick, its pieces are either both even (two even sticks) or both odd (none). Either way the new position has an odd number of sticks and at most two even sticks: it is in B.

Remove k sticks of length k. If k is odd, an odd number of sticks leaves, so the count flips from even to odd; only odd-length sticks leave, so the even-stick count stays at most one. If k is even, removing k even sticks would need at least k ≥ 2 even sticks, but A has at most one even stick. No such removal exists from A. Every legal move from A therefore lands in B.

From B there is always a way back

B has an odd number of sticks and 0, 1 or 2 even sticks.

0 even. Every stick is odd. If some stick is longer than 1, break it: it becomes one even and one odd piece, so the count is even and there is exactly one even stick — A. If every stick is 1, remove one 1-stick (the k = 1 removal): the count is even and no even stick is left — A.

1 even. Split the even stick into two odd pieces (2 = 1 + 1, 4 = 1 + 3, 6 = 3 + 3, and so on). The count becomes even and the even stick is gone — A.

2 even. Split one of them into two odd pieces. The count becomes even and one even stick remains — A.

So B is never a dead end.

Why the second player wins

The first player starts in A and must move to B. The second player replies from B to A. The empty board is in A, so the second player is the one who moves into it and makes the last move. This is an invariant argument: A is the losing side of the two-set split, also called the set of P-positions.

The logic test checks it as a fact, not just as the page’s claim. It looks at every position with total length at most 21 and no stick longer than 11 — 3,222 positions, 594 in A and 989 in B. From every A position every legal move lands in B, and from every B position some legal move lands back in A. Solving the game independently agrees that A is exactly the losing set and B exactly the winning set. The start is losing for N = 1 to 12, and in 240 played-out games a human making any random legal move loses to the computer from every N = 1 to 30.

The computer is the applet’s own Play method, written a second time from the bytecode. The two versions are compared with the same random draws on all 3,222 positions, on every start N = 1 to 30 and on all 2,315 positions reachable from the starts for N = 1 to 8; the resulting position, the kind of move and the number of random draws agree.

Press Computer starts with N = 1. After the computer’s first move you are the second player: find a move back to A, and keep finding one. Then try N = 10. If you move anywhere else, the computer can take the second-player role for itself.
